subtopic_detail: Stratifying a complex adnexal mass in a postmenopausal woman to decide the surgical pathway
stem:
A 62 year old woman attends your practice with three months of abdominal bloating, feeling full after small meals and a vague dragging discomfort in the pelvis. She has lost 4 kg without trying.

She went through menopause at 50 and has had no bleeding since. Her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness, and bimanual examination reveals a firm irregular mass arising from the pelvis. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Her bowel habit is unchanged and a faecal occult blood test arranged by a colleague was negative. The imaging and tumour marker you requested have now returned.

data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, firm irregular pelvic mass, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Ultrasound: 9 cm multilocular right adnexal mass with solid areas and internal vascularity, moderate ascites, normal endometrial thickness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy at the local hospital next month
options.rationale: Cystectomy is an operation for a benign cyst in a woman wishing to preserve ovarian tissue, and performing it here risks rupturing a malignant cyst and upstaging the disease. Fertility preservation is not a consideration at this age. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound and tumour marker in three months to see if they change
options.rationale: Interval surveillance is appropriate for a simple unilocular cyst under 5 cm with a normal marker in a postmenopausal woman. With solid areas, ascites and a markedly raised marker, a three month delay allows progression of a disease whose outcome depends on early complete surgery. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Arrange image guided percutaneous biopsy of the mass before any referral
options.rationale: Percutaneous sampling of an apparently operable ovarian mass risks seeding the peritoneum and the needle track, and the diagnosis is normally made at definitive surgery instead. Biopsy is reserved for advanced disease where chemotherapy will precede surgery. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer to the general gynaecology list for laparoscopic oophorectomy locally
options.rationale: Survival in ovarian cancer depends strongly on complete cytoreduction performed by a trained subspecialist, and operating outside such a unit is associated with incomplete staging and worse outcomes. The referral destination is itself part of the treatment decision. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Calculate the risk of malignancy index and refer to gynaecological oncology
options.rationale: The index combines menopausal status, ultrasound morphology and the CA125 value, and a score above 200 identifies a high probability of malignancy warranting referral to a specialist centre. Her postmenopausal status, multiple suspicious ultrasound features and markedly raised marker place her far above that threshold. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer presents with vague abdominal symptoms such as bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency and pelvic discomfort, and the persistence and newness of these symptoms in a woman over 50 is what should trigger investigation rather than their individual specificity. Initial assessment combines pelvic ultrasound with serum CA125, and these feed with menopausal status into the risk of malignancy index, where a score above 200 indicates referral to a gynaecological oncology centre. The reason the referral destination matters so much is that survival correlates with the completeness of cytoreduction achieved at the first operation, which is consistently better in specialist units. CA125 must be interpreted with care, since it rises in endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, pregnancy and any peritoneal irritation, which is why the index weights it alongside imaging rather than using it alone.
key_points: Persistent new bloating and early satiety over 50 warrant investigation
Initial assessment is pelvic ultrasound plus serum CA125
The risk of malignancy index combines menopausal status, ultrasound and CA125
A score above 200 mandates referral to a gynaecological oncology unit
Survival depends on complete cytoreduction at the first operation
explanation.pearls: CA125 is raised in only about half of early stage ovarian cancers, so a normal value never excludes malignancy in a woman with a suspicious mass on ultrasound.

subtopic_detail: Choosing intrapartum prophylaxis when the recorded penicillin reaction is a delayed childhood rash
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar asked to write up intrapartum antibiotics for a woman at 39 weeks who is 4 cm dilated with intact membranes. Her screening swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus.

Her notes carry an allergy label for penicillin. When you ask her about it directly, she describes a flat blotchy rash over her tummy and back that appeared three or four days into a course of amoxicillin for a sore throat when she was about six years old. It settled over a week without treatment. She has never had swelling of the lips or tongue, wheeze, faintness or blistering, and she has taken cephalexin for a urinary infection since then without trouble.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, foetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Screening: Vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks positive for group B streptococcus, susceptibility not requested
data_table.Allergy history: Delayed maculopapular rash on day three or four of amoxicillin at age six, no mucosal or respiratory involvement, subsequent cephalexin tolerated
data_table.Labour: Cervix 4 cm dilated, membranes intact, contracting three in ten minutes

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin despite the allergy recorded in her notes
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin is the agent of choice where no allergy exists, and a delayed rash is indeed low risk, but a recorded penicillin label is not simply overridden at the bedside in labour without formal assessment. The cephalosporin achieves comparable cover while respecting the label. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin because she reports an allergy to penicillin
options.rationale: Vancomycin is reserved for women at high risk of anaphylaxis whose isolate is resistant to clindamycin or whose susceptibility is unknown, and it crosses the placenta less reliably. Using it for a low risk rash history exposes mother and baby to a broader agent without benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin because her reported reaction was not severe
options.rationale: A delayed maculopapular rash without mucosal, respiratory or systemic involvement is a low risk history, and the cross reactivity between penicillins and cefazolin is negligible because they share no side chain, which her subsequent tolerance of cephalexin supports. Cefazolin crosses the placenta well and achieves adequate foetal levels, making it the preferred choice in low risk allergy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous clindamycin without testing the isolate for susceptibility
options.rationale: Clindamycin is an option only for severe allergy and only when the isolate has been shown susceptible, since resistance rates in group B streptococcus are appreciable and no susceptibility was requested here. Giving it blind risks ineffective prophylaxis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin once labour is established and repeated six hourly
options.rationale: Prophylaxis must be intravenous to achieve adequate and rapid amniotic fluid concentrations before birth, and the oral route cannot do this reliably. It also ignores the recorded allergy to the same drug class. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis prevents early onset neonatal group B streptococcal sepsis and is most effective when the first dose is given at least four hours before birth. Benzylpenicillin is first choice, and the decision tree for a woman with a penicillin label turns entirely on how severe the reported reaction was. A low risk history is an isolated delayed rash without mucosal involvement, systemic features or blistering, and such women receive cefazolin, which shares no side chain with the penicillins and carries negligible cross reactivity. A high risk history, meaning anaphylaxis, angioedema, respiratory compromise or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction, moves the choice to clindamycin if the isolate is proven susceptible and otherwise to vancomycin. Because most penicillin allergy labels are inaccurate, taking a proper allergy history in the antenatal period is a concrete clinical intervention rather than a formality.
key_points: Benzylpenicillin is first line when no allergy label exists
Severity of the reported reaction determines the alternative chosen
Delayed rash without systemic features is a low risk history
Cefazolin shares no side chain with penicillins and is preferred in low risk allergy
Clindamycin requires demonstrated susceptibility of the isolate
explanation.pearls: Request clindamycin susceptibility at the time of the 36 week group B streptococcus swab for any woman with a penicillin allergy label, because the result is unavailable once she presents in labour.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Deciding on a repeat antenatal corticosteroid course four weeks after the first when birth again appears likely
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a woman at 30 weeks and 2 days who has been readmitted with regular painful contractions and a cervix that has shortened on transvaginal scan since her last assessment.

She was admitted four weeks ago with threatened preterm labour, received a complete course of betamethasone then, and settled without giving birth. On that occasion the contractions stopped within a day. This time her contractions are stronger and more frequent, her cervical length has fallen considerably and the consultant judges that birth within the next week is likely. Her membranes are intact, her observations are normal and there is no evidence of infection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 90/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, foetal heart rate 144/min
data_table.Previous treatment: Complete betamethasone course given four weeks ago at 26 weeks and 2 days
data_table.Current findings: Cervical length 12 mm on transvaginal ultrasound, contracting three in ten minutes, membranes intact
data_table.Investigations: White cell count and C reactive protein within normal limits, glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate decision regarding corticosteroids?

options.text: Give a full new two dose course every week until she gives birth
options.rationale: Weekly repeated courses have been associated with reduced birthweight and smaller head circumference without additional respiratory benefit, so repetition is deliberately limited. The evidence supports a single repeat rather than a rolling schedule. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Withhold repeat steroids because a course has already been given
options.rationale: The benefit of the original course wanes after about seven days, so a woman who did not give birth within that window and now faces imminent birth stands to gain from a repeat. Treating the first course as permanently sufficient forfeits that benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Withhold repeat steroids because she is now beyond 30 weeks gestation
options.rationale: The accepted gestational ceiling for a repeat course extends beyond 30 weeks, so this gestation does not exclude her. Respiratory morbidity remains substantial at this gestation and the treatment still reduces it. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Give a repeat course only once the membranes have actually ruptured
options.rationale: Membrane rupture is neither necessary nor sufficient as a trigger, since the decision rests on the likelihood of birth within the next seven days. Waiting for rupture may mean the course is given too late to take effect. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Give a single repeat course as birth is likely within the next week
options.rationale: A single repeat course is indicated when more than seven days have elapsed since the first, the woman remains below the gestational ceiling and birth is judged likely within the next seven days, all of which apply here. The Australian randomised evidence showed reduced respiratory distress and less oxygen requirement with a single repeat, without the growth effects seen with weekly dosing. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

explanation.summary: A single course of antenatal betamethasone before preterm birth reduces respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage and neonatal death, and the effect is greatest when birth occurs between 24 hours and seven days after the course. The clinical difficulty arises with the substantial group of women who receive a course during a threatened preterm labour that then settles, and who represent again weeks later. Australian randomised evidence established that a single repeat course in that situation reduces respiratory morbidity, whereas weekly repetition reduces birthweight and head circumference without further respiratory gain. The decision therefore requires three conditions together: more than seven days since the previous course, a gestation still within the treatable range, and a genuine judgement that birth is likely within the next week. Corticosteroids also raise maternal blood glucose for several days, which matters when diabetes complicates the pregnancy.
key_points: Maximal benefit falls between 24 hours and seven days after administration
A single repeat course is supported when more than seven days have elapsed
Weekly repeated courses reduce birthweight and head circumference
The judgement that birth is likely within seven days is part of the indication
Maternal blood glucose rises for several days after a course
explanation.pearls: Australian practice was shaped by a randomised trial showing that one repeat betamethasone course reduced neonatal respiratory morbidity, which is why the repeat is offered once rather than on a weekly schedule.

subtopic_detail: Matching alcohol relapse prevention pharmacotherapy to a goal of reduced drinking rather than abstinence
stem:
A 45 year old carpenter attends your general practice asking for help with his drinking. He describes about ten standard drinks most evenings, morning shakiness that settles once he has a drink, and two failed attempts to cut down on his own.

He is clear that he does not want to stop completely at this stage but wants to get the amount down, and he will not consider an inpatient admission. He takes no regular medication, uses no opioids and has never injected drugs. His liver enzymes are mildly raised at twice the upper limit of normal with a normal bilirubin and normal synthetic function, and his renal function is within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: No stigmata of chronic liver disease, no asterixis, no peripheral neuropathy
data_table.Liver function: Alanine aminotransferase 82 U/L (less than 45), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (less than 20), albumin and international normalised ratio within normal limits
data_table.Other: Renal function within normal limits, no current opioid use, declines inpatient withdrawal

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is most appropriate to offer him now?

options.text: Acamprosate started once he has completed a supervised withdrawal
options.rationale: Acamprosate works by maintaining abstinence once it has been achieved and requires the patient to have stopped drinking first, which he has declined to do. It has little effect on the quantity consumed in someone still drinking. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.text: Disulfiram with supervised dosing arranged through his pharmacy
options.rationale: Disulfiram depends on an aversive reaction to any alcohol at all and therefore requires a committed abstinence goal with supervision, making it unsuitable for someone who intends to keep drinking. Using it here would risk a deliberate and dangerous reaction. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.text: Naltrexone started now while he continues to drink at a reduced level
options.rationale: Naltrexone blocks the opioid mediated reward of drinking and reduces heavy drinking days and the quantity consumed, so it suits a harm reduction goal and does not require prior abstinence. His mildly raised transaminases with preserved synthetic function are not a contraindication, and he uses no opioids. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.text: Baclofen at high dose titrated against his reported craving levels
options.rationale: Baclofen is a later option used mainly where liver disease precludes the first line agents, and the evidence for it is weaker with a risk of sedation and of a withdrawal syndrome on abrupt cessation. His liver function does not force that choice. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.text: Topiramate titrated slowly as first line pharmacotherapy for craving
options.rationale: Topiramate has some supporting evidence but is not registered for this indication in Australia and carries cognitive slowing and paraesthesiae that limit tolerability. It sits behind the established first line agents. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

explanation.summary: Pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder is chosen by matching the drug to the patient's stated goal rather than by ranking the drugs against each other in the abstract. Naltrexone reduces the reinforcing effect of alcohol and therefore reduces heavy drinking days, which makes it the agent of choice when the goal is reduced consumption or when the person is still drinking at the point of prescribing. Acamprosate stabilises glutamatergic transmission after withdrawal and is used to maintain an abstinence that has already been achieved, so it presupposes a completed withdrawal. Disulfiram requires both a firm abstinence goal and supervision to be safe and effective. All three sit alongside psychosocial support rather than replacing it, and a stated harm reduction goal is a legitimate clinical target rather than a failure of motivation.
key_points: Naltrexone reduces heavy drinking and does not require prior abstinence
Acamprosate maintains an abstinence that has already been achieved
Disulfiram requires a committed abstinence goal and supervised dosing
Concurrent opioid use contraindicates naltrexone and must be asked about
Pharmacotherapy supplements rather than replaces psychosocial treatment
explanation.pearls: Naltrexone will precipitate withdrawal in anyone taking opioids and blocks opioid analgesia, so document a plan for acute pain and advise the patient to carry that information before the first dose.

sources.label: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems
